summary: A widow repeatedly confronts an unjust judge until he grants justice; Jesus uses the contrast to teach persistent prayer and confidence that God hears the oppressed. A Pharisee and tax collector pray at the temple: one converts real practices into comparison and self-exaltation, while the other asks God for mercy and goes home justified. Jesus receives infants as models of dependent kingdom reception. A wealthy ruler asks about eternal life, claims commandment fidelity, and cannot accept the invitation to sell, give to the poor, and follow; what is humanly impossible remains possible with God. Jesus predicts his Jerusalem suffering again (as at 9:22 and 9:44), but the Twelve understand none of it. Near Jericho, a blind beggar persists in calling the Son of David until Jesus stops, restores sight, and turns the road into praise.
whyItMatters: Luke places powerless persistence beside privileged confidence. God is not the unjust judge, and humility is not self-hatred; prayer entrusts justice, mercy justifies, children receive, possessions are relinquished, and silenced people keep crying until the road itself changes.

context.author: The Gospel's anonymous author, traditionally Luke, grouping prayer parables, children, wealth, passion prediction, and a Jericho healing near the journey's end
context.audience: Theophilus and a wider Greek-reading audience; in the chapter, disciples tempted by delay, spiritual comparison, status, wealth, and silencing need
context.date: Commonly dated after Jerusalem's destruction in AD 70, around AD 80–90; dates in the 60s and into the early second century are also defended; part of the travel narrative
context.setting: Imagined court, Jerusalem temple prayer, Jesus's road, approach to Jericho, and the anticipated ascent to Jerusalem
context.literaryForm: Contrast parables, pronouncement stories, call dialogue, passion prediction, and healing with acclamation

outline.heading: Persistent widow and unjust judge
outline.note: A judge who fears neither God nor man defends a widow who keeps coming; God, says Jesus, will quickly avenge his chosen

outline.heading: Pharisee and tax collector at prayer
outline.note: A Pharisee thanks God he is not like others; a tax collector beats his chest and says 'God, be merciful to me, a sinner'.

outline.heading: Infants received and kingdom reception
outline.note: People bring babies for him to touch; the disciples rebuke them, but Jesus says 'Allow the little children to come'.

outline.heading: Rich ruler, possessions, impossibility, and reward
outline.note: Told to sell all, a rich ruler grows sad; a camel through a needle's eye, Jesus says, is easier than a rich man entering

outline.heading: Third Jerusalem passion prediction misunderstood
outline.note: He tells the twelve the Son of Man will be mocked, scourged and killed, and rise on the third day; they understand none

outline.heading: Blind beggar cries out, sees, follows, and sparks praise
outline.note: A blind man near Jericho cries 'have mercy on me' and, rebuked, shouts louder; Jesus gives him sight, and he follows glorifying God

keyVerses.text: I tell you, this man went down to his house justified rather than the other; for everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, but he who humbles himself will be exalted.”
keyVerses.why: God's verdict overturns comparative self-righteousness at the place of prayer.

keyVerses.text: Most certainly, I tell you, whoever doesn’t receive God’s Kingdom like a little child, he will in no way enter into it.”
keyVerses.why: Kingdom is received from dependency rather than possessed as status or achievement.

keyVerses.text: But he said, “The things which are impossible with men are possible with God.”
keyVerses.why: The wealthy man's impasse is not softened, yet impossibility is not given the final word.

questions.question: Is God like the unjust judge?
questions.answer: The parable argues from lesser to greater: if a shameless judge finally responds, how much more will the just God vindicate chosen people who cry day and night. Delay remains emotionally real, but God's character is contrast, not equivalence. Persistent prayer refuses both despair and private vengeance.

questions.question: What social power does the widow have?
questions.answer: Israel's law singles out widows for protection (Exodus 22:22; Deuteronomy 10:18). Her only narrated resource is repeated presence and speech. The judge fears neither God nor people, yet her persistence wears down a judge who would ignore her.

questions.question: Is the Pharisee condemned for fasting and tithing?
questions.answer: Those practices can be faithful. The problem is his prayer ‘by himself,’ gratitude built on contempt, and a moral inventory used to rank him above ‘the rest of men.’ Jesus criticizes self-exaltation within Jewish prayer, not Judaism or disciplined devotion as such.

questions.question: What does the tax collector mean by ‘be merciful’?
questions.answer: He uses hilaskomai, which elsewhere can mean to atone for sin; here it is a plea: ‘be merciful,’ or be propitious, to me. He does not present works, excuses, or comparison. On one common reading, Luke's ‘justified’ is a divine verdict restoring right standing, not the man's claim that exploitation never needs repair.

questions.question: What quality of children receives the kingdom?
questions.answer: Luke says infants were being brought, emphasizing dependence and inability to confer status or repay. The text does not specify innocence, cuteness, or curiosity as the one trait. Receiving like a child means accepting God's reign as gift from a position without leverage.

questions.question: Why does Jesus tell this ruler to sell everything?
questions.answer: The command exposes the attachment controlling this particular obedient, wealthy man and directs assets to the poor before calling him to follow. Luke consistently makes possessions a discipleship issue. Readers debate whether every disciple must liquidate all property, but the passage itself ties the demand to riches (18:24).

questions.question: Was there a tiny gate called ‘the Needle's Eye’?
questions.answer: No reliable ancient evidence supports the popular small-gate explanation. Jesus uses comic impossibility: a camel through a sewing needle. The hearers understand and ask who can be saved; Jesus answers with God's possibility, not a technique for squeezing rich people through while keeping their baggage.

questions.question: Why does the blind man keep shouting when rebuked?
questions.answer: The crowd treats his voice as disruption, but he recognizes Jesus as Son of David and intensifies his plea. Jesus stops, asks what he wants rather than assuming, restores sight, and receives him as a follower. The story models accessible attention and refuses to let gatekeepers define whose need may reach the road.

glossary.def: Grant justice or publicly set right, the widow's repeated request.
Declared or shown to be in right standing before God.
To be merciful or propitious; the tax collector asks this of God (18:13).
Royal messianic title used by the blind beggar as Jesus approaches Jerusalem.
